metadata.description: Evidence-based rehabilitation phase templates for sports injuries. Based on systematic review of rehabilitation frameworks from PubMed and Consensus research.

goals: Control pain and swelling (PRICE/PEACE protocol)
Protect injured tissue from further damage
Maintain range of motion within pain-free limits
Preserve cardiovascular fitness with non-painful activities
Reduce muscle inhibition / atrophy
Patient education on injury and recovery timeline
Psychological support: address fear of re-injury
criteria_to_progress: Pain at rest ≤ 2/10
Significant reduction in swelling
Pain-free or near-pain-free active range of motion
Able to perform daily activities without significant limitation
Full weight-bearing (for lower limb injuries) with minimal pain
loading_principles: Isometric exercises are preferred - provide analgesic effect without joint movement
Pain allowed ≤ 3/10 during gentle ROM exercises
Avoid loading positions that stress the healing tissue under tension
Aquatic therapy provides early loading with reduced weight-bearing forces
BFR training can be initiated early to reduce quad atrophy (e.g. post-ACLR)
phase_templates.clinical_notes: Based on evidence from van Melick et al. 2016 (PMID via DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2014-093474) and rehabilitation role in sport injury consensus (Defi 2023). The PEACE & LOVE framework (Protection, Elevation, Avoid anti-inflammatory modalities, Compression, Education / Load, Optimism, Vascularization, Exercise) represents the current evidence-based approach replacing older RICE/PRICE protocols.

goals: Restore full pain-free range of motion
Begin progressive loading of injured tissue
Rebuild muscle strength and endurance
Restore proprioception and neuromuscular control
Maintain or improve cardiovascular fitness
Address contributing biomechanical deficits
Normalize movement patterns
criteria_to_progress: Full pain-free active and passive ROM
Injured limb strength ≥ 60-70% of contralateral limb
Good quality neuromuscular control during closed-kinetic-chain exercises
No pain with moderate-intensity activities
For lower limb: able to walk normally, jog straight-line
loading_principles: Progressive overload: increase sets/reps/load every 1-2 weeks
Pain monitoring: allow up to 4/10 pain during exercise that returns to baseline within 24 hours
For tendinopathies: isometric → isotonic → eccentric → heavy slow resistance progression
Closed kinetic chain exercises preferred for knee injuries (less ACL stress than OKC)
Eccentric training emphasized: reduces injury recurrence rates for hamstring and Achilles
Frequency: 3-5 sessions per week; allow 48h recovery between resistance sessions
phase_templates.clinical_notes: This phase spans the inflammatory-to-proliferative tissue healing transition. Evidence from Bourne et al. 2018 (PMID 29116573, DOI 10.1007/s40279-017-0796-x) supports eccentric exercises for hamstring strengthening. HSR protocol (Liu et al. 2026, PMID 42192475) demonstrates patellar tendinopathy management. Alfredson eccentric protocol (PMID 37628466, 36538166) remains gold standard for Achilles tendinopathy rehabilitation.

goals: Achieve injured limb strength ≥ 85% of contralateral (Limb Symmetry Index)
Introduce sport-specific movement patterns
Progressive plyometric loading
High-speed running and direction changes
Restore confidence in the injured area
Address psychological readiness for sport return
Develop sport-specific power and endurance
criteria_to_progress: Limb Symmetry Index ≥ 85-90% on strength testing
No pain with any rehabilitation exercises
Successful completion of single-leg hop test battery (≥90% LSI)
Ability to run at 85-90% maximum speed pain-free
Good quality cutting and change of direction
Psychological readiness score ≥ 7/10 on ACL-RSI or equivalent
loading_principles: Progressive plyometric introduction: bilateral jumps → unilateral → reactive plyometrics
Running progression: linear → curved → lateral → cutting/sprinting
Load monitoring: rate sport as 1-10, target return to 7 before full sport
Training load: controlled increase (≤10% weekly volume increase recommended)
On-field rehabilitation: 4 pillars - movement quality, physical conditioning, sport-specific skills, training load development (Buckthorpe et al. 2019)
Nordic Hamstring Exercise introduced in this phase for hamstring injury prevention
phase_templates.clinical_notes: Key reference: Buckthorpe et al. 2019 (Consensus result) on on-field rehabilitation. For ACL: criteria-based progression with LSI testing is the evidence standard per van Melick 2016. Nordic Hamstring Exercise demonstrated 64-65% reduction in hamstring injury incidence (van der Horst 2015, PMID 25794868). Copenhagen adductor exercise for groin: PMID 26750142.

goals: Full return to unrestricted sport participation
Achieve symmetric performance to pre-injury level
Injury prevention screening and ongoing monitoring
Return to competition with confidence
Establish ongoing maintenance program to prevent recurrence
criteria_to_progress: Limb Symmetry Index ≥ 90% on all functional tests (hop tests, strength testing)
Psychological readiness: ACL-RSI ≥ 65 (for ACL) or equivalent score
Successful completion of sport-specific clearance testing
Pain-free sprinting at 100% (mandatory for hamstring injuries)
Movement quality assessment: clinician sign-off on landing and cutting mechanics
Minimum time criterion met (e.g. ≥9 months post-ACLR per van Melick guidelines)
loading_principles: Full sport load introduction over 2-4 weeks of graduated team participation
Progress from individual drills → small group → full training → competitive play
Ongoing strength maintenance: minimum 1 session/week to prevent deconditioning
Re-testing at 1, 3, 6, and 12 months post-return to detect early recurrence
Psychological preparation: graduated exposure, visualization techniques

strength_tests: Isokinetic knee extension strength (target ≥90% LSI at 60°/s and 180°/s)
Single-leg calf raise (≥30 reps and symmetric)
psychological: ACL-Return to Sport Index (ACL-RSI) ≥65 for ACL injuries
Fear-Avoidance Beliefs Questionnaire if elevated fear
Athlete self-report confidence ≥8/10 for sport-specific activities

phase_templates.clinical_notes: Return-to-sport criteria are multifactorial. Evidence from van Melick 2016 mandates 9-12 month post-ACLR rehabilitation with combined strength + hop tests + psychological assessment. Paton et al. 2023 Delphi (Consensus, 78.3-98.3% agreement) for hamstring: pain-free sprinting is mandatory criterion. Schwank et al. 2022 (Bern Consensus) provides shoulder RTS framework. Aquatic therapy (PMID 38992731) may accelerate return timelines for ankle sprains.
